title: Prostrations
hookLine: full-length bows, done by the hundred and thousand

lines: A BOW THAT LEAVES NOTHING STANDING.
FLAT ON THE GROUND, ARMS AHEAD.
cards: There's a kind of bow that leaves nothing standing. Palms come together. The knees go down, the hands slide forward along the ground, and the whole body lies flat, forehead to the floor, arms stretched ahead.
A breath. Then all of it reverses, back to standing. And then, in temples and quiet shrine rooms in Tibetan Buddhist communities, people do it again, and again.
Some keep a pair of smooth wooden boards under their hands so they can slide. Back on day two, you bowed three times, to the three jewels. Today, the bow that uses the whole body.

teach.b: First, how it's done. In Tibetan teachings the joined palms often touch three places before the body goes down: the crown, the throat, the heart.
Teachers link them to body, speech and mind, so the bow is the whole person, offered. Second, why the body. Pride is something you can feel in your posture: chest out, chin up, standing over things.
A full prostration is the body doing the opposite, on purpose.
Teachers call it a remedy for pride, and say the mind tends to follow where the body goes. Third, by the hundred and the thousand.

teach.h: BOWED WITH REFUGE, OVER AND OVER.
teach.b: In the Tibetan foundational practices, which tomorrow opens up, prostrations are done together with taking refuge, the turn met earlier with the lamrim.

Practitioners picture the Buddha, the teaching and the community in front of them, and bow to them. Tradition sets a very large number, and people work through it over months or years, a session at a time.
Some pilgrims even travel by prostration, measuring a road with the length of their own bodies. Fourth, all the way down. A half bow stops where it's comfortable.

teach.h: TO THE FLOOR, AND UP AGAIN.
teach.b: This one goes to the floor, where there's no further to fall. Then it gets up.
Teachers point out that rising matters as much as going down: you return to standing, lighter, and begin again.

how: Tibetan Buddhists do full-length prostrations in temples, shrine rooms and on pilgrimage, often reciting refuge while they bow, and as part of the foundational practices students complete them in large numbers over months or years.

o: a deep nod of the head used to greet a teacher
full-length bows, the whole body laid flat on the ground
kneeling silently at a shrine for a whole session

games.q: you're starting the foundational practices. you know how to prostrate. what do you bow toward?
o: the refuge: the Buddha, the teaching and the community.
your own reflection in the shrine-room window.
games.why: in the foundational practices, prostrations go together with taking refuge: practitioners picture the three jewels ahead and bow to them.

practice: If your body allows it, do three prostrations on a clear patch of floor: palms to crown, throat and heart, then kneel, slide your hands forward, lie flat for one breath, and come back up slowly.
If a full bow isn't right for your knees or your back, kneel and bow your forehead toward the floor, or simply bow your head where you sit. Then rest in the stillness after the third.

wordCard.voice: Prostrations. Full-length bows, the whole body to the ground, done over and over in Tibetan practice. Today's word.

orig.note: Tibetan chaktsal: to prostrate, to pay homage. It's the word for this bow, and it opens many Tibetan verses of praise.

carryVoice: Your line: all the way down. And all the way up again. Day thirteen-oh-four, done.
